place: Arkaroola Wilderness Sanctuary, northern Flinders Ranges, South Australia, Australia
summary: Arkaroola is a wildlife sanctuary in the northern Flinders Ranges that Mars Society Australia selected as a Mars analog region. Its site report says the case rested on a mix of logistical convenience and scientific value, including a fossil hydrothermal system around Mount Painter and the Paralana hot springs. A research station called Mars-Oz was proposed for the gravel plains east of the zone.
terrain_geology: The area has rugged ranges, a fossil hydrothermal system with an alteration halo, and the Paralana hot springs, which are radioactive and heated without a magma source.
climate: The area has a subtropical desert climate under the Koppen system.
access_and_facilities: Most visitors arrive by car, and flights can be chartered from Adelaide. The sanctuary has a village and a network of four-wheel-drive tracks.
hazards: Radon gas collects near the Paralana springs and prolonged stays there may be a health hazard.

place: Askja caldera, Dyngjufjöll mountains, central highlands, Iceland
summary: Askja is an active volcano in a remote part of the central highlands of Iceland. It is a complex of nested calderas inside the Dyngjufjöll mountains. NASA used the area to train Apollo astronauts in geology before the lunar missions.
terrain_geology: The central volcano holds several nested calderas, including the main summit caldera, a smaller caldera to its north-east, and the lake-filled caldera formed in the late nineteenth century. Most eruptions from the system are small, basaltic and effusive.
climate: Askja lies in the rain shadow north-east of the Vatnajökull glacier, so rainfall is low for Iceland.
access_and_facilities: The central volcano region can only be reached for a few months of the year.
hazards: It is an active volcano with a long record of eruptions, and the area is cut off by snow for much of the year.

place: Yungay area, Atacama Desert, Antofagasta Region, Chile
summary: The Atacama is a plateau desert on the Pacific coast of northern Chile, and the area around the abandoned Yungay mining town is commonly called the driest place in the world. The desert has been used for Mars expedition simulations, and NASA uses it to test instruments for future Mars missions. In a published test, researchers repeated the Viking life-detection experiments on Yungay-region soil and found no signs of life.
terrain_geology: Soils in parts of the Atacama have been compared to Martian soil. Perchlorates, which were also found on Mars by the Phoenix lander, occur in the desert along with nitrate deposits that contain organics.
climate: Rain is almost absent. Some places have gone years without any, and some weather stations have never recorded rain. A marine fog called camanchaca supplies moisture to some locations.
access_and_facilities: The University of Antofagasta Desert Research Station is located near the Yungay area in the Antofagasta Region.
hazards: Rare heavy rain has triggered deadly mudflows in the region.

place: Maria Elena South, Atacama Desert, Antofagasta Region, Chile
summary: Maria Elena South is a hyperarid site in the Atacama Desert, near the former nitrate mining town of Maria Elena. Researchers reported it as much drier than the better-known Yungay site and as a better Mars-like environment. Soil in the wider Atacama has been compared with Martian soil, and NASA uses the desert to test instruments for future Mars missions.
terrain_geology: The desert is a low-relief bench, like a giant uplifted terrace, with evaporite formations and large deposits of nitrate, iodine-bearing minerals, copper and lithium.
climate: A cold desert climate with mild temperatures through the year. Some weather stations in the desert have never recorded rain.
hazards: Rare rain can cause flash floods and mudflows, and some areas support no plant or animal life at all.

place: Gypsum Hill and Lost Hammer springs, Axel Heiberg Island, Nunavut, Canada
summary: Axel Heiberg Island is an uninhabited island in the Canadian High Arctic. Lost Hammer is a cold, very salty, oxygen-poor spring that flows up through thick permafrost. Researchers study it as an analog for possible Martian subsurface brines and methane, and the McGill Arctic Research Station on the island has been used for Mars analog work. The sources read describe Lost Hammer in detail but say little about Gypsum Hill.
terrain_geology: The spring emerges through a gypsum and anhydrite diapir and builds a hollow salt tufa cone that empties and refills with the seasons.
climate: Polar, with continuous permafrost and winter darkness from roughly October to February.
access_and_facilities: The island has no permanent residents. The McGill Arctic Research Station sits inland from Expedition Fiord and operates from March to August.

place: Barranco del Jaroso (Jaroso ravine), Sierra Almagrera, Almeria province, Spain
summary: The Jaroso ravine is the type locality of the mineral jarosite, first described there by August Breithaupt. Researchers have proposed its hydrothermal system as a model for Mars exploration because jarosite was later detected on Mars by the Opportunity rover. It has also been used to test Raman, laser-induced breakdown and Mossbauer instruments on Mars-relevant minerals.
terrain_geology: The range rose from the seabed along many faults that later filled with lead and silver ore veins. Alunite-group minerals, including jarosite and natrojarosite, dominate the ravine.
access_and_facilities: The range lies near the Mediterranean coast within the municipality of Cuevas del Almanzora. It is part of an EU protected area for its flora and fauna.

facts.label: Year mining of the range resumed

place: Beacon Valley and University Valley, Quartermain Mountains, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Victoria Land, Antarctica
summary: Beacon Valley is an ice-free valley in the Quartermain Mountains of Victoria Land, part of the McMurdo Dry Valleys. University Valley is a small side valley that drains into it. Researchers describe the high-elevation Dry Valleys as one of the closest Earth matches for Martian ground ice, because dry permafrost sits over ice-cemented ground.
terrain_geology: The valley floors are mostly bare, loose gravel with ice-wedge polygons. Ice lies a short distance under the surface, as massive ground ice in middle Beacon Valley and as ice-cemented ground under dry permafrost in University Valley.
climate: The Dry Valleys are a cold desert shaped by katabatic winds and a snow shadow behind the Transantarctic Mountains. At the higher sites, air temperatures stay below freezing.
access_and_facilities: The valleys are inside a specially managed Antarctic area and are reached from the McMurdo Station region by research programmes.
hazards: Extreme cold and wind, and strict environmental protection rules apply.

place: Bockfjord volcanic complex, Bockfjorden, Spitsbergen, Svalbard, Norway
summary: The Bockfjord Volcanic Complex is a group of volcanic centres on the western side of Bockfjorden in northern Spitsbergen, including Sverrefjellet and Sigurdfjellet. The Arctic Mars Analog Svalbard Expedition (AMASE) works here to adapt instruments for Mars life-detection missions. Carbonate globules in the volcanic rocks resemble those in a well-studied Mars meteorite, and how they formed is still debated.
terrain_geology: Rock types include basalt, peridotite xenoliths and clays, with hot-spring travertines and carbonate globules in basalt. The area also has warm springs, subsurface ice and sedimentary red beds.
access_and_facilities: Field teams based themselves in Ny-Alesund or aboard a research vessel, with helicopter support.

place: Bodele Depression, northern Chad
summary: The Bodele Depression is a dry lake basin at the southern edge of the Sahara in northern Chad. Its floor is made of fine diatom sediment left by the former Mega-Lake Chad, and it is one of the strongest dust sources on Earth. The sources we read do not describe it as a Mars analog; GSOP lists it as a candidate not in our reference list because of its dust output.
terrain_geology: A dry basin between the Tibesti and Ennedi mountains. Exposed lakebed sediment, including fossil diatoms, breaks down into fine dust.
climate: Strong low-level winds are channelled between the two mountain ranges and raise dust, most often from October to March.
access_and_facilities: Faya-Largeau is the largest nearby town. We found no other access information.
hazards: Frequent dust storms, including a major event that reached West Africa and the Cape Verde Islands.

place: Bunge Land (Zemlya Bunge), New Siberian Islands, Sakha Republic, Russia
summary: Bunge Land is a flat, sandy and almost bare plain between Kotelny and Faddeyevsky islands in the New Siberian Islands, off the northern coast of Siberia. Most of it floods during storm surges, and it has almost no vegetation or people. The page read does not describe any analog use, so its place on our list rests on GSOP's own screening as a candidate not in our reference list.
terrain_geology: The surface is sandy and very flat, with a small slightly higher area in the southeast.
access_and_facilities: Uninhabited, with no facilities listed in the source read.
hazards: Storm surges flood most of the surface.

place: Channeled Scablands and Dry Falls, central Washington, United States
summary: The Channeled Scablands are bare basalt channels and basins carved by repeated glacial outburst floods. Planetary scientists regard them as perhaps the best terrestrial analog of Martian outflow channels. Dry Falls is a dry cataract in the Scablands that is easy to visit and shows the scale of the flood erosion.
terrain_geology: Floods stripped the loess cover and exposed basalt, leaving a pattern of linked channels, coulees, cataracts and rock basins. Dry Falls is a scalloped cliff with four large alcoves and plunge pools at its base.
access_and_facilities: Dry Falls can be viewed from an interpretive center in Sun Lakes-Dry Falls State Park, on the state route near Coulee City. Parking needs a Discover Pass.

place: Chott el Djerid, between Tozeur and Kebili, central Tunisia
summary: Chott el Djerid is a large salt lake in central Tunisia and the largest salt pan of the Sahara. It is flat and covered with salt crust, and it dries out almost completely in summer. In this project it is a candidate not in our reference list, and the sources checked here do not document planetary analog use.
terrain_geology: The lake bottom is a flat evaporite basin that appears in shades of white, green and purple at different times.
climate: The climate is hot desert, with very little rain and strong summer sunshine that evaporates the water.
access_and_facilities: The towns of Tozeur and Kebili sit on its edges. The lake can be crossed on foot or by car, and a road crossing exists, but the salt crust is not always firm.
hazards: The salt crust can give way, which makes crossing off the roads dangerous.

place: Concordia Station, Dome C, Antarctic Plateau, Antarctica
summary: Concordia is a French-Italian research station on the Antarctic Plateau, and it is one of the coldest places on Earth. During winter the crew is cut off from the outside world, with no transport and limited communication. That extreme isolation and confinement resembles long space missions, so the station is used for space medicine research and regularly hosts ESA scientists.
terrain_geology: The station sits on an ice dome of the Antarctic Plateau.
climate: Polar ice cap climate, frigid all year round.
access_and_facilities: Most cargo arrives by overland traverse from Dumont d'Urville Station. The station is inaccessible in winter and needs total autonomy.
hazards: Extreme cold and months of complete isolation during winter.

place: Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, Idaho, USA
summary: Craters of the Moon is a large basaltic lava field on the Snake River Plain in central Idaho. Apollo astronauts trained there to find and collect rock samples in a harsh, unfamiliar setting. In its first field deployment, NASA's BASALT research programme ran simulated spacewalks on the lava flows as an analog for present-day Mars.
terrain_geology: Three lava fields along the Great Rift, with basalt flows, cinder cones, lava tubes, tree molds and deep open rift cracks.
climate: Dry and cold at altitude, with snowy winters and hot summers. Dark lava surfaces get much hotter than the air in summer.
access_and_facilities: The monument lies along US highways between the towns of Arco and Carey. A single paved loop road and a first-come campground serve visitors, and the loop road closes to cars in late November because of snow.
hazards: No backcountry water, sharp lava and loose rock in caves, and extreme summer heat and winter cold.

facts.label: Craters of the Moon lava field area

place: Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, Idaho, USA
summary: Craters of the Moon is a large basaltic lava field in south-central Idaho with cinder cones, lava flows and lava tubes in one area. Apollo astronauts trained there to find and collect rock samples. The source also notes that the Moon's craters are mostly from impacts while these formed by eruptions, so the match is partial.
terrain_geology: The lava field is the largest mostly Holocene basaltic field in the contiguous United States, built along a long volcanic rift with many cones and a long lava tube.
climate: Cold, semi-dry winters with heavy snow and warm summers.
access_and_facilities: Highways cross the northwest corner. One paved loop road serves the monument, with a visitor center at its entrance and a campground. The loop road closes to traffic in late November because of snow.
hazards: There is no backcountry water, lava is sharp, cave entrances need scrambling, and the area is dormant rather than extinct.

place: Cuatro Cienegas basin, Coahuila, Mexico
summary: Cuatro Cienegas is a desert basin with hundreds of spring-fed pools, gypsum soils and stromatolites. NASA-linked studies treat its microbial mats and desert aquatic habitats as a way to think about early Mars, and NASA Earth Observatory notes that it is gypsum-rich like the sediment mound at Gale crater. Researchers link its microbial diversity to a shortage of phosphorus.
terrain_geology: The basin holds gypsum-rich soils and dunes, springs, pools and marshes at the eastern edge of the Chihuahuan Desert.
climate: The area is a desert with little rain, and water stress may grow as rainfall falls and evaporation rises.
access_and_facilities: The town of Cuatro Cienegas is the municipal seat, and the basin is a biosphere reserve with a protected flora and fauna area inside it.

place: Dallol hydrothermal system, Danakil Depression, Afar region, Ethiopia
summary: Dallol is a hydrothermal system around a small volcano in the Danakil Depression of Ethiopia. It is known for strange colours and mineral patterns and for some of the most acidic spring fluids on Earth. Researchers call it a poly-extreme site and a key system for astrobiology, because acid, salt and heat occur together.
terrain_geology: Basaltic magma pushed into old salt deposits and built a salt dome with hot springs, small geysers and salt canyons. Iron and other impurities give the surface its yellow, ochre and brown colours.
climate: The area is among the driest and hottest on the planet, and it is one of the lowest land points on Earth.
access_and_facilities: Travel guides say the Danakil Depression cannot be visited independently, and escorts and permits are needed.
hazards: The springs discharge very hot, strongly acidic brines, and the vents release carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide and sulfur dioxide.

place: Ubehebe Crater and the basin floor, Death Valley National Park, California, USA
summary: Northern Death Valley has a volcanic crater field and a salt pan in one national park. NASA has used Death Valley as a Mars analog since it prepared for the Viking missions. Ubehebe Crater has been compared to Gale Crater, and researchers study the salt pan as a model for salt deposits that may have formed on Mars as water disappeared.
terrain_geology: Ubehebe is a maar, a crater formed by a steam-driven eruption, ringed by a tuff deposit with black ash on the rim. A playa lake lies on the crater floor.
access_and_facilities: The craters are inside Death Valley National Park and open to visitors, a long drive from Furnace Creek and Las Vegas.
hazards: The risk of renewed volcanic activity is low.

place: Dhofar desert near Marmul, Dhofar Governorate, Oman
summary: The Austrian Space Forum ran its AMADEE Mars simulation in the Dhofar desert in southern Oman, with a field camp near the Marmul outpost. The mission tested engineering, surface operations, astrobiology, geology and life science experiments. Reports say the terrain resembles several Martian surface features, including sedimentary structures and salt domes.
terrain_geology: Desert plain below a semicircle of mountains, with sedimentary structures and salt domes reported at the field site.
climate: The governorate has a tropical climate with a summer monsoon season called the khareef, and winters can bring dust storms.
access_and_facilities: Salalah, the governorate capital, has an international airport and a large seaport. Oman signed an agreement with the Austrian Space Forum to host the mission.
hazards: Winter dust storms and sudden temperature drops from northern winds.

place: Don Juan Pond, Wright Valley, Victoria Land, Antarctica
summary: Don Juan Pond is a very small, extremely salty pond at the western end of Wright Valley in the Antarctic Dry Valleys. Its calcium chloride brine stays liquid at very low temperatures, which is why it is studied for what brines could do on Mars. The source read says research here may inform study of similar saline settings on other bodies.
terrain_geology: The pond sits between the Asgard and Dais ranges, ringed by salt crusts left as water evaporated. Researchers debate whether its brine comes from shallow deliquescence or from deep groundwater.
access_and_facilities: The nearest listed settlement is Vanda Station, to the east.

place: Dumont Dunes, Mojave Desert, California, United States
summary: Dumont Dunes is a field of large sand dunes in the Mojave Desert. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory drove Scarecrow, a stripped-down twin of the Curiosity rover, here to prepare for sand-trap driving in Gale crater. More recently the laboratory used it as a secondary site for drone navigation tests aimed at future Mars rotorcraft.
terrain_geology: The dunes sit beside the slow Amargosa River and are bordered by steep volcanic hills.
climate: The low elevation makes spring and summer warm to extremely hot.
access_and_facilities: The site is reached from the state highway north of Baker and is a federal off-highway vehicle recreation area run by the Bureau of Land Management.

place: Dunhuang Yardang National Geopark, Gansu province, China
summary: This geopark in Gansu province holds the largest field of yardangs in China. Yardangs are ridges that wind carves from soft rock, and they also occur on a very large scale on Mars. The sources checked here do not describe Mars analog fieldwork at this park, so the link is the landform type, not a documented programme.
terrain_geology: Wind and rain have eroded the soft ground and left harder rock standing as ridges, many named for the shapes they resemble. The formations took a very long time to develop.
access_and_facilities: The geopark lies north-west of the town of Dunhuang. The sources checked give the distance but no route or visitor details.

place: Emi Koussi, Tibesti Mountains, Borkou Region, Chad
summary: Emi Koussi is a large shield volcano at the southeast end of the Tibesti Mountains and the highest mountain in the Sahara. Two nested calderas cap it, and a smaller caldera called Era Kohor holds sodium carbonate deposits. It has been studied as an analogue of the Martian volcano Elysium Mons. This comparison is a candidate in our screening and is not in our reference list.
terrain_geology: Alkaline lavas, ignimbrites, lava domes, cinder cones and maars cover the volcano. The floor of Era Kohor is white with sodium carbonate and holds a salt lake. Fumaroles and hot springs are still active at the southern foot.
climate: Desert mountain climate. No weather stations are close to the summit, so rainfall there is estimated from cloud cover.
access_and_facilities: The region is remote and access is difficult for political reasons. Dirt roads cross the western and eastern margins of the summit caldera.
hazards: Volcanism in the area is poorly studied, and fumarole and hot spring activity continues.

place: Erfoud and Merzouga, Errachidia Province, Draa-Tafilalet, Morocco
summary: Erfoud is an oasis town on the Saharan edge of Morocco, close to the Erg Chebbi dunes at Merzouga. The Austrian Space Forum ran a month-long Mars analog field simulation near Erfoud, including work at the Kess Kess formation, a set of old mud mound structures. Wikipedia notes that the terrain around Erfoud is used for Mars analog research.
terrain_geology: Desert edge with large Erg Chebbi dunes, and the Kess Kess mud mound structures of Devonian age near Erfoud.
access_and_facilities: Merzouga is a village with hotels and restaurants for visitors, a short drive from Erfoud and Rissani. Mission support during the simulation was run from Innsbruck, Austria.
hazards: Flash floods struck Merzouga in an earlier year and displaced many residents.

place: Sa Grutta cave, Supramonte, Sardinia, Italy
summary: ESA CAVES is an astronaut training course held underground in the Supramonte area of Sardinia, with the Sa Grutta cave used as basecamp. ESA describes caves as a space analog for working in teams where safety is critical, and the course is as much about teamwork as technical caving. Crews have included astronauts from several space agencies. The sources read do not describe the cave as a lava tube.
access_and_facilities: The course starts with a preparation week and then moves underground, where the team sets up a basecamp in the cave.

facts.label: Typical time spent underground per course

place: Fiskenaesset anorthosite complex, near Qeqertarsuatsiaat (Fiskenaesset), Sermersooq municipality, southwestern Greenland
summary: The Fiskenaesset complex is a metamorphosed layered intrusion that is rich in anorthosite. Older studies found similarities between its plagioclase and lunar plagioclase, but also differences, and an older Greenland geological survey report cautioned against drawing planetary conclusions from the comparison. A recent conference abstract reports a pink spinel rock there that matches lunar spinel in composition and texture; that abstract has not been peer reviewed in the sources we found.
terrain_geology: Anorthosite occurs as conformable layers within high-grade gneisses.
access_and_facilities: The nearest settlement is Qeqertarsuatsiaat, also called Fiskenaesset, on an island off the Labrador Sea coast.

facts.label: Year of the pink spinel conference abstract

place: Fukushima Robot Test Field, Minamisoma, Fukushima Prefecture, Japan
summary: The Fukushima Robot Test Field is a facility in Minamisoma for testing robots on land, at sea and in the air. The University of Aizu has built a simulated lunar crater there as part of its Moon/Mars Garden concept, to test robot movement and communication. The organisers plan to open it to outside users as a testbed.
terrain_geology: The lunar area is a built crater covered with a lunar soil analogue, not a natural geological feature.
access_and_facilities: The field sits in the Minamisoma reconstruction industrial park and was built under the Fukushima Innovation Coast Framework. The university plans to open the lunar analog area to potential users.

place: Gosses Bluff (Tnorala), Tnorala Conservation Reserve, Northern Territory, Australia
summary: Gosses Bluff, known as Tnorala to the Western Arrernte people, is the eroded remnant of an impact crater in central Australia. The ring of hills seen today is the exposed central uplift of a much larger original crater. Our reference list uses it as an analog for central-peak structure on the Moon, but we did not find a source that describes it as a lunar analog.
terrain_geology: The ridge is made of fractured and brecciated sandstone and shale. Shatter cones are the strongest evidence of an impact origin.
access_and_facilities: The site lies in the Tnorala Conservation Reserve, west of Alice Springs. It is a sacred place to the Western Arrernte.

place: Grand Canyon, South Rim and inner canyon, Arizona, USA
summary: The Grand Canyon is a very deep gorge cut by the Colorado River through thick rock layers. Apollo astronauts took geology field trips here in the early years of the programme to learn to read rock layers. The canyon is geologically very different from the Moon, so it is a training site more than a surface look-alike.
terrain_geology: Stacked sedimentary layers on the rim, such as the Kaibab Limestone, above very old schist at the bottom of the inner gorge.
climate: The inner gorge is hot in summer, while the rims have cold winters with heavy snow. The South Rim is drier than the North Rim.
access_and_facilities: Grand Canyon Village on the South Rim has hotels, including El Tovar, and a railway station.
hazards: Dehydration, heat, hypothermia, winter storms, summer thunderstorms and rockfall.

place: Harrat Khaybar and Umm Jirsan lava tube, Hejaz region, Saudi Arabia
summary: Harrat Khaybar is a large field of basaltic lava north of Medina in Saudi Arabia, with cinder cones, lava flows and the country's longest known lava tube system, Umm Jirsan. The sources read describe its geology and archaeology but do not describe it as an analog site. Its place on our list is a GSOP screening result, a candidate not in our reference list.
terrain_geology: Lava has erupted along a long north-south line of vents, with pale comendite domes in the White Mountains and darker hawaiite flows elsewhere. Jabal Qidr is a scoria cone listed among IUGS geological heritage sites.

place: Haughton impact crater, Devon Island, Nunavut, Canada
summary: Haughton is an impact crater on Devon Island in the Canadian High Arctic. The Haughton-Mars Project, run by SETI and the Mars Institute and funded mainly by NASA, uses the crater and surrounding terrain as a planetary analog, in particular for the Moon and Mars. The Mars Institute describes Devon Island as the largest continuous area of barren rocky polar desert on Earth.
terrain_geology: The impact peeled back shale and siltstone to expose the gneissic basement, and material from deep below the surface has been identified. Valley networks, canyons, gullies and old lake beds surround the crater.
climate: Temperatures stay below freezing for much of the year, and weathering is slow. Devon Island is far milder than Mars.
access_and_facilities: The site is remote, and the project runs a research station on the island each summer.

place: Haughton impact crater, Devon Island, Nunavut, Canada
summary: Haughton is an impact crater on Devon Island in the Canadian Arctic. The Haughton-Mars Project, run by the Mars Institute and the SETI Institute with NASA support, uses the crater to test the challenges of living and working on Mars. The Mars Society also operates the Flashline Mars Arctic Research Station at the crater.
terrain_geology: The impact removed much of the shale and siltstone and exposed the older basement rock, and the crater centre holds impact breccia that is frozen with permafrost. Cold and slow weathering keep features that craters at lower latitudes lose.
climate: At this latitude temperatures stay below freezing for much of the year. The Mars Institute calls Devon Island the largest continuous area of barren rocky polar desert on Earth.
access_and_facilities: The project base has stood at its present location since early in the century. The sources checked do not describe how the site is reached.

place: HI-SEAS habitat, Mauna Loa, Island of Hawaii, USA
summary: HI-SEAS is a small dome habitat on the slope of Mauna Loa where crews of six lived in isolation for simulated Mars missions. NASA's Human Research Program funded follow-up studies for several years, and the site is now operated by the International MoonBase Alliance. The sources we read describe the area as isolated with Mars-like features.
terrain_geology: A barren volcanic slope far from other buildings, described as having Mars-like features.
access_and_facilities: The habitat is a two-floor dome with an attached shipping container that holds supplies, water and power systems.
hazards: The altitude slightly raises radiation exposure, and one mission was halted after a crew member suffered an electric shock.

place: Holuhraun lava field, Icelandic Highlands, Iceland
summary: Holuhraun is a basaltic lava field just north of the Vatnajokull ice cap in the Icelandic Highlands. It grew in a recent fissure eruption (dates in the facts), so much of it is very fresh. The page read gives no Mars or Moon analog statements, so the analog case here comes from GSOP's reference list rather than from that source.
terrain_geology: Lava lies at the southern end of the Odadahraun lava desert, with the Dyngjujokull outlet glacier immediately to the south and the Askja caldera to the north.
access_and_facilities: An unnumbered track crosses the field and joins a gravel highland road at both ends.
hazards: Glacial outburst floods have repeatedly affected the area.

place: Hopi Buttes volcanic field, near Dilkon, Navajo Nation, northeastern Arizona, United States
summary: The Hopi Buttes are a field of small volcanoes on the Colorado Plateau. In the years before the first lunar landing, USGS and NASA personnel tested early Apollo spacesuits and a lunar flying vehicle here. It was one of several nearby volcanic sites visited during Apollo preparation, and the sources we found do not rank it above Cinder Lake or Sunset Crater for crater training.
terrain_geology: The field has about three hundred maars and diatremes. Eastern parts show shallowly eroded maar deposits, and western parts show deeper-eroded feeder diatremes.
access_and_facilities: The field lies mostly on the Navajo Reservation, north of Holbrook.

place: Extraterrestrial landing test site, Huailai County, Hebei province, China
summary: This is China's test facility for landing spacecraft on other bodies, in Huailai County, Hebei. It uses tall tether towers to reduce the load on a lander, which mimics low gravity, and a cratered field to mimic rough terrain. It was used for a Mars lander hover and obstacle test and, more recently, for a landing and takeoff test of the Lanyue crewed lunar lander.
terrain_geology: The field is a built test area with craters and tether towers, not a natural analog.
access_and_facilities: It is a restricted aerospace facility. One report says it is run by the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation. Details of the site are only partly published.

facts.label: Mars lander hover and obstacle test

place: Tolbachik volcano area, Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia
summary: Tolbachik is a basaltic volcanic complex on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia's Far East. A Brown University presentation lists tests in Kamchatka among the Lunokhod rover test activities, and a travel blog says the Soviets tested their first lunar rover at Tolbachik. The Planetary Society also reported that ash from earlier eruptions was good for testing Mars rover mobility. We did not find a primary Soviet-era source for the lunar tests at this exact spot.
terrain_geology: The volcano produced a large basaltic fissure eruption that built several cinder cones, and a later eruption left lava caves. Fumarole deposits are a source of rare minerals.
hazards: Fast-moving basaltic lava flows have reached inhabited areas.

place: Kamil crater, East Uweinat Desert, New Valley Governorate, Egypt
summary: Kamil is a small, young impact crater in the far southwest of Egypt, close to the Sudan border. It has a well-preserved ray system, which Wikipedia describes as rare among craters on Earth. It was located on satellite imagery and later confirmed on the ground; we found no source calling it an established Moon analog, and GSOP lists it as a candidate not in our reference list.
terrain_geology: An iron meteorite struck sandstone bedrock, and sand now covers part of the crater. Thousands of meteorite fragments were collected.
access_and_facilities: The crater is very remote and lies close to the Sudan border. A geophysical expedition reached it for fieldwork.

place: Karakul impact structure and lake, Pamir Mountains, Tajikistan
summary: Karakul is a large, brackish lake that fills an impact crater high in the Pamir Mountains of Tajikistan. The crater is young in geological terms, though its age is still uncertain. The sources read do not describe it as an analog site, so its place on our list is a GSOP screening result, a candidate not in our reference list.
terrain_geology: The lake has no outlet and is surrounded mostly by pasture, with marshes, wet meadows and pebbly and sandy plains.
access_and_facilities: A small village of the same name lies on the eastern shore, and the area is inside Tajik National Park.

place: Kaunertal Glacier, Tyrol, Austria
summary: The Austrian Space Forum ran a two-week Mars simulation on the Kaunertal Glacier (dates are in the facts). Analog astronauts in Aouda spacesuit simulators worked with robotic vehicles under a mission support center in Innsbruck. The forum chose the site for its access and its small-scale terrain resembling Mars where water ice is present, and describes it as the highest-altitude analog mission it has run (a claim by the organizers).
terrain_geology: The site is a rock glacier and glacier in the Alps, studied with ground-penetrating radar and glacier microbial life detection.
access_and_facilities: A toll road runs up the valley to the base of the glacier ski area, and the base station sat near the end of it.

place: Kilauea summit caldera and Kaʻū Desert, Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, Hawaiʻi, USA
summary: Kilauea is an active basaltic volcano on the island of Hawaiʻi, and the Kaʻū Desert lies on its south-west flank. NASA used the area to train Apollo astronauts to recognise volcanic features, plan traverses, collect samples and take photographs. Astronauts from several Apollo landing missions used this training on the Moon.
terrain_geology: The Kaʻū Desert surface is dried lava remnants, volcanic ash, sand and gravel. The summit caldera holds a pit crater called Halemaʻumaʻu.
climate: The Kaʻū Desert gets more than a metre of rain a year, so it is not a true desert, and the rain turns acidic when it mixes with volcanic sulfur dioxide.
access_and_facilities: Both areas are in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, which has one hotel and restaurant inside it. Parts of the park close during high volcanic activity.
hazards: Hazards include volcanic gas, acid rain, ash, explosions and lava; the park closes areas when gas blows toward them.

place: Kilbourne Hole, Potrillo volcanic field, Dona Ana County, New Mexico, USA
summary: Kilbourne Hole is a maar, a volcanic crater formed by a steam-driven eruption, in the Potrillo volcanic field of southern New Mexico. NASA trained Apollo astronauts in lunar geology here, and a later NASA field team tested instruments for future missions and simulated moonwalks in the hole.
terrain_geology: The rim cliffs are basalt with clear columnar jointing, and the ejecta holds many fragments of mantle and lower crust rock. Sand dunes sit on the east side, and a dry lakebed lies on the crater floor.
access_and_facilities: The hole is in Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks National Monument, reached by a county road west of the railroad. Much land inside the hole is private, and collecting rocks is illegal.

place: Kolyma Lowland, Sakha Republic (Yakutia), Russia
summary: The Kolyma Lowland is a flat plain of marshes and lakes in northeast Siberia with a subarctic climate. Its ice-rich Pleistocene permafrost, known as Yedoma, holds well-preserved organic matter, fossils and ancient DNA. We did not find a source that calls it a Mars analog; GSOP lists it as a reference for life preserved in ground ice.
terrain_geology: A lowland plain between the Alazeya and Yukagir plateaus, with thick fine-grained, ice-rich permafrost deposits.
climate: Subarctic. We found no temperature or rainfall figures in the sources we read.
hazards: Ice-rich permafrost can sink badly when it thaws.

facts.label: Largest reported thaw subsidence in northeast Siberia

place: Kumtag Desert, near Dunhuang, Gansu and Xinjiang, China
summary: Kumtag is a large sandy desert in northwestern China that borders Dunhuang. News reports say China tested its Yutu lunar rover in this desert before launch, and an official said it was the most suitable of the deserts surveyed. The rover later landed on ground that was rougher than the test terrain.
terrain_geology: Drift-sand dunes can be very tall along the desert ranges, and the southern rim is a maze of hills.
climate: Winds blow mostly from the west and northwest, and some scrubby plants get water only once in several years.
access_and_facilities: A news report placed the rover tests in the desert some distance from Dunhuang city.

facts.label: Rover test site distance from Dunhuang (2011 report)

place: Matanomadh area, Kutch, Gujarat, India
summary: A team from SAC-ISRO, IIT Kharagpur and NGRI reported jarosite near Matanomadh (first report year in the facts) and argued the setting resembles Martian jarosite sites. A later paper in American Mineralogist identified the mineral as natrojarosite, the sodium variant. It reports natrojarosite and associated sulfates that point to acidic, water-limited conditions, which the authors call analogous to the Noachian-Hesperian period of Mars.
terrain_geology: The area is a basalt-hosted setting in the Palaeocene Matanomadh Formation, with natrojarosite, natroalunite, kaolinite and anhydrite.
climate: The mineral assemblage is consistent with an oxidizing environment and periodic shifts between humid and arid conditions.
access_and_facilities: The site is northwest of Bhuj in Kutch.

facts.label: Distance northwest of Bhuj (press reports, 85 to 86)

place: Tso Kar basin and Puga Valley, Rupshu, Changthang, Ladakh, India
summary: Tso Kar is a high-altitude salt lake in the Changthang region of southern Ladakh. Researchers have studied Puga hot spring deposits and Tso Kar brine together as possible Mars analogs. ISRO and Protoplanet built the HOPE analog station at Tso Kar to simulate Moon and Mars conditions.
terrain_geology: Tso Kar has no outflow, and the evaporating saline water leaves white salt crusts along its margins. At Puga, spectroscopy has found borate minerals with halite and opaline silica, and sulfate minerals alongside crystalline sulfur.
climate: Winters are extreme and summers are warm with large daily swings. Rain and snow are very rare, and the basin sits in a rain shadow.
access_and_facilities: The Leh to Manali road passes west of the lake, and roads from Miru reach its shores. A tented camp stands on the west bank.
hazards: Extreme cold, thin air and strong ultraviolet radiation.

facts.label: Distance of Leh to Manali road west of lake

place: Lake Gilmore, Goldfields-Esperance region, Western Australia, Australia
summary: Lake Gilmore is an acidic, ephemeral salt lake in southern Western Australia. Researchers study it and similar lakes because their interbedded clays and sulfates resemble Martian geochemistry. A modeling study found that the Meridiani Planum area shares acidic saline water, sulfates and iron minerals with these lakes, with some differences.
terrain_geology: Acid playa sediments include clay minerals and sulfates, and the minerals jarosite and alunite occur at Lake Gilmore and two other Western Australian dry lakes.
climate: Hot, dry summers and cool winters at the nearest climate station, in Salmon Gums.

place: Timanfaya National Park, Lanzarote, Canary Islands, Spain
summary: Timanfaya is a national park of fresh volcanic terrain on the southwest of Lanzarote. ESA has used Lanzarote for the geology course that trains astronauts for work on the Moon, Mars and asteroids. Press reports also say NASA and ESA have tested rovers on the island's lava fields.
terrain_geology: Entirely volcanic ground formed mostly by eruptions that lasted several years in the early eighteenth century, with craters, lava fields and lava tubes. Surface rock is very hot just below ground.
access_and_facilities: Visitors park at a public car park and tour by coach on a road closed to private traffic. Two footpaths need prior authorisation and a guide.
hazards: Very hot ground close to the surface, and strictly controlled access to protect plants and animals.

place: Timanfaya National Park and La Corona lava tube, Lanzarote, Canary Islands, Spain
summary: Lanzarote is a young volcanic island, and Timanfaya National Park covers fresh basalt lava and cones from historic eruptions. ESA's PANGAEA course has used the island for years to train astronauts in field geology and astrobiology for Moon and Mars exploration, including visits to Timanfaya and the La Corona lava tube. ESA notes that underground structures such as lava tubes are good shelters from radiation.
terrain_geology: The park is made entirely of volcanic soil from large eruptions in the early eighteenth century, with the most recent activity in the early nineteenth century.
access_and_facilities: A car park serves a coach tour on a road otherwise closed to the public, and two footpaths need prior authorization and a guide.
hazards: The ground near the core of the park is very hot just below the surface.

place: Lava Beds National Monument, Siskiyou and Modoc counties, northeastern California, United States
summary: Lava Beds is a protected area on the flank of Medicine Lake Volcano with the highest concentration of lava caves in North America. NASA's BRAILLE project used it to practice cave exploration with a test rover called CaveR, as preparation for lunar and Martian lava tubes. Lava tubes could shelter Moon bases from radiation, and on Mars they could protect possible life.
terrain_geology: The monument sits where three physiographic provinces meet and has many lava tubes, cave collapse trenches and high desert shrubland.
access_and_facilities: Many caves have marked entrances and developed trails for the public. Lowering a rover through a skylight remains a hard problem for tube exploration.

place: Licancabur volcano, Chile and Bolivia border, Central Andes
summary: Licancabur is a stratovolcano on the Chile and Bolivia border. Its summit crater holds a small freshwater lake, one of the highest lakes in the world. Researchers have studied the area because conditions at its lakes resemble those believed to have existed in former Martian lakes.
terrain_geology: The cone is built on older ignimbrites and is made mainly of andesite, with steep slopes from viscous lava. Lava flows reach far from the summit.
climate: It is cold, dry and windy, with low air pressure and large swings between day and night. There are no glaciers and snow cover is temporary.
access_and_facilities: Climbers usually approach from the Bolivian side. The town of San Pedro de Atacama lies to the west.
hazards: It is a potentially active volcano with no known historical eruption. The upper cone is steep and unstable, and bad weather can arrive quickly.

place: Lonar crater, Buldhana district, Maharashtra, India
summary: Lonar is a meteorite impact crater in the flood basalt of the Deccan Traps, and it holds a saline, alkaline lake. Its ejecta layers show radial movement and forms described as similar to those seen on Mars. A university study also reported soil minerals resembling Apollo lunar rocks. It is a national geological monument and a Ramsar wetland.
terrain_geology: The host rock is Deccan basalt. The crater rim rises a little above the surrounding land, and the lake sits in a basin with no outflow.
climate: Monsoon climate with dry deciduous forest around the crater.
access_and_facilities: The crater is next to the town of Lonar in Buldhana district.
hazards: Farm chemicals, littering and sewage pollute the lake, and illegal logging and mining have changed the local ground.

place: Lop Nur, Ruoqiang County, Xinjiang, China
summary: Lop Nur is a former salt lake on the eastern edge of the Tarim Basin, between the Taklamakan and Kumtag deserts. The dry basin is covered by a thick salt crust, and satellite images show the concentric shorelines of the vanished lake. We found no source that uses it as a Mars analog; GSOP lists it as a candidate not in our reference list.
terrain_geology: A flat, dry lake basin with a salt crust and ring-shaped old shorelines. The lake dried as water was diverted and rivers shifted.
access_and_facilities: A provincial highway from Hami and a railway serve the area. Some parts are under military management and closed to the public.
hazards: Very remote terrain where two explorers died while walking across it, and a former nuclear test base lies nearby.

place: Lunar Crater volcanic field, Nye County, Nevada, USA
summary: Lunar Crater volcanic field is a dry basaltic field in central Nevada with lava flows, scoria cones, tuff rings and four maars. Wikipedia says it has been used to test prototype Mars rovers and to train astronauts for the Moon landings. Lunar Crater itself is a National Natural Landmark.
terrain_geology: The field has many small volcanoes, lava flows and a near-circular maar called Lunar Crater, set around a dry lake bed.
climate: Continental and dry.
access_and_facilities: Two highways pass through the field and dirt roads cross it, with parking at Easy Chair and on the rim of Lunar Crater. Tonopah is the nearest named town in the source.

place: Lunodrom near Simferopol, Crimea
summary: The lunodrom was a rover training track near Simferopol, built to test the Lunokhod rover frame and to train the engineers who drove it. Drivers with no earlier vehicle experience learned to control a machine on another body, allowing for signal delay. Crimea is internationally recognised as part of Ukraine but has been controlled by Russia since the annexation.
terrain_geology: Descriptions of the course mention craters, ditches, trenches, boulders, gravel walls and sandy slopes.
access_and_facilities: Sources disagree on the exact site: some name Shkolnoye (a former closed town), others the village of Shkilne northwest of Simferopol. Current access is not documented in the sources we read.

facts.label: Year Russia took control of Crimea

place: Makhtesh Ramon, Negev desert, near Mitzpe Ramon, Israel
summary: Makhtesh Ramon is a large erosional depression in Israel's Negev desert. The Austrian Space Forum, the Israel Space Agency and the Israeli group D-MARS ran an Austrian Space Forum Mars analog mission there, with a crew of six analog astronauts. Reports describe the crater's geology as similar to Mars in several respects.
terrain_geology: The basin holds clay hills in red and yellow tones, a black basalt hill, dark intrusive rock, quartzite hills and vertical dikes. Rocks on the floor are very old, and the basin formed when rivers carved the softer rock after the Arava rift valley opened.
access_and_facilities: The small town of Mitzpe Ramon sits on the northern edge, and a visitor centre is run by the Israel Nature and Parks Authority. The mission crew lived in a purpose-built solar-powered habitat.

place: Mars Desert Research Station, near Hanksville, San Rafael Swell, Utah, USA
summary: The Mars Desert Research Station is a habitat run by the Mars Society in the Utah desert, chosen for its Mars-like terrain and appearance. Crews live in the habitat and wear spacesuit simulators outside while they practice field tactics, habitat design and crew selection. Research there includes microbes in local rocks and desert soils.
terrain_geology: The desert was chosen for its Mars-like terrain and appearance. The source we read does not describe the rock layers in detail.
climate: The site is much warmer than Mars. Crew rotations run in the northern winter, and the field season ends in spring because of desert heat.
access_and_facilities: The station is northwest of Hanksville by road. Crews reach field destinations on foot or by all-terrain vehicle.
hazards: Desert heat limits the field season.

place: Mars Desert Research Station, near Hanksville, Utah, USA
summary: The Mars Desert Research Station is a small habitat run by the Mars Society on the San Rafael Swell in southern Utah. Volunteer crews live and work there in simulated Mars missions, and a NASA-funded teacher training programme there simulates living on the Moon or Mars. The desert was chosen for its Mars-like terrain.
terrain_geology: Desert terrain chosen for its Mars-like appearance. Rock-dwelling microbes called endoliths are often studied there.
climate: Much warmer than Mars. The field season ends in northern spring because of desert heat.
access_and_facilities: Hanksville is the nearest town, reached by road. Crews walk or use all-terrain vehicles for outings, and water is rationed.
hazards: A fire once destroyed the original greenhouse, and part of the site is a foot-traffic-only zone.

place: Mauna Kea and PISCES test sites, Hawaii Island, Hawaii, USA
summary: Mauna Kea is a dormant shield volcano on Hawaii Island whose volcanic cinder and tephra have been used as a stand-in for lunar soil. PISCES, a center at the University of Hawaii at Hilo, prepared a Mauna Kea test site for NASA field demonstrations of the RESOLVE in-situ resource experiment, which looked for hydrogen and water in the soil. The sources read disagree on the exact altitude of the test site, so the summit figures below describe the mountain, not the test pad.
terrain_geology: The summit area has small cinder and pumice cones and lava domes built partly during past glaciations.
climate: Alpine at the summit, with frost common all year and snow possible from the middle elevations up.
access_and_facilities: Saddle Road eased travel to the mountain, and summit access is restricted.
hazards: Altitude sickness is a risk at high elevation.

place: McMurdo Dry Valleys (Taylor and Wright valleys), Victoria Land, Antarctica
summary: The McMurdo Dry Valleys are the largest ice-free region of Antarctica and the coldest, driest desert in the world. Researchers treat them as the best known Earth analog of the Martian high northern plains where Phoenix landed, and as an astrobiology stand-in for Mars. The sources we read describe a Mars analog use; none of them describe a lunar cold-trap use.
terrain_geology: The valleys have granite and gneiss bedrock, glacial till and loose gravel. The upper permafrost is dry rather than ice-cemented, which resembles Martian soil.
climate: Katabatic winds scour away snow and humidity, and evaporation and sublimation exceed precipitation. Above a certain elevation the air stays at or below freezing.
access_and_facilities: The valleys lie within the McMurdo Valleys Antarctic Specially Managed Area, so access is managed.

place: Merriam Crater cinder deposits, San Francisco volcanic field, near Flagstaff, Arizona, USA
summary: Merriam Crater is a cinder cone in the San Francisco volcanic field near Flagstaff, Arizona. NASA's JSC lunar mare soil simulants were mined from a commercial cinder quarry on the crater's flank. The later version was designed to match an Apollo mare soil sample.
terrain_geology: The material is glass-rich basaltic ash that approximates the chemistry, mineral content, grain size and engineering behaviour of lunar mare soil. For the later version the ash was milled and sieved with no chemical processing.
access_and_facilities: The source is a commercial quarry, and the simulant was made available to qualified investigators. The exact quarry position differs slightly between sources.

facts.label: Apollo sample matched by the JSC-1A simulant

place: Mistastin (Kamestastin) Lake crater, Labrador, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
summary: Mistastin is a confirmed impact crater in northern Labrador, filled by a lake with an arc-shaped central island that is the crater's central uplift. It is used for field geology training of Canadian Space Agency and NASA astronauts. A doctoral thesis treats it as a lunar science and exploration analogue.
terrain_geology: The target rock was a batholith of adamellite and mangerite with lenses of anorthosite. Shock features include shatter cones, melt rocks and glass.
access_and_facilities: The site is within the traditional hunting grounds of the Mushuau Innu First Nation, and visiting requires permission.

place: Moses Lake sand dunes, Quincy Basin, Washington, USA
summary: The Moses Lake dunes are a field of basaltic sand in the Quincy Basin of central Washington. NASA used the dunes in an earlier year to test prototype robots, rovers, cargo carriers, cranes and spacesuits for future lunar missions. NASA's JPL describes the field as the largest basaltic wind-blown sand accumulation on Earth.
terrain_geology: Wind-blown sand made mostly of basalt fragments, with some quartz. Dunes on the east side are still active.
access_and_facilities: The dunes are southwest of the town of Moses Lake. The test team worked in an open treeless area with room for large equipment.

place: Mount Erebus, Ross Island, Antarctica
summary: Mount Erebus is an active volcano on Ross Island with a long-lived lava lake in its summit crater. Dante I, an eight-legged tethered walking robot, was taken to the crater rim there in a NASA and National Science Foundation project to develop technology for future Moon or Mars trips. The descent stopped when the fiber-optic cable was severed.
terrain_geology: The volcano is a composite cone with a shield-like lower half, and its summit holds a persistent phonolite lava lake inside an inner crater.
access_and_facilities: The American McMurdo Station and the New Zealand Scott Base are on the same island.
hazards: A sightseeing passenger aircraft crashed into the mountain, killing all aboard, and the ice caves can hold air with a high carbon dioxide share.

place: Mount Etna, Metropolitan City of Catania, Sicily, Italy
summary: Mount Etna is an active stratovolcano whose lava fields and granular surface have been used to test robots for lunar missions. The Helmholtz ROBEX analog mission ran there first, and the German Aerospace Center later led the ARCHES demonstration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and ESA (dates are in the facts). In that demonstration an ESA astronaut drove the Interact rover remotely from Catania.
terrain_geology: Etna is built of basaltic lava and ash above the boundary between the African and Eurasian plates.
access_and_facilities: The volcano is near Catania, and the ARCHES operators worked from a control site in Catania, whose distance from the volcano is in the facts.
hazards: Etna is one of the most active volcanoes in the world and is almost constantly active.

place: Mount Howe, east side of Scott Glacier, Marie Byrd Land, Antarctica
summary: Mount Howe is an elongated mountain near the head of Scott Glacier in Marie Byrd Land, apparently the southernmost mountain in the world. It is a rocky outcrop in the polar ice. In this project it is a candidate not in our reference list, and the sources checked here do not document planetary analog use.
terrain_geology: It consists of low connecting ridges and gable-shaped rock peaks that stick up through the ice.
climate: The area has no net annual snow accumulation. The source gives no temperature data.
access_and_facilities: The Mount Howe area has the closest blue ice runway to the South Pole, where wheeled aircraft can land.

facts.label: First seen by Byrd Antarctic Expedition

place: Myvatn and Namafjall, northern Iceland
summary: Myvatn is a shallow lake in a volcanically active part of northern Iceland, with rootless cones (pseudocraters) formed when lava met wet sediment and caused steam explosions. Nearby Namafjall has hot springs and fumaroles that alter basalt into clays and iron sulfates. Researchers have proposed Namafjall deposits as an analogue for sulfate soils at Gusev crater, and rootless cones have been compared with cones seen on Mars from orbit.
terrain_geology: The lake formed after a large basaltic lava eruption. The shore has groups of pseudocraters and lava pillars, and Namafjall is a ridge of hyaloclastite.
climate: Tundra climate with cool summers and long, cold winters.
hazards: The area has active volcanism and earthquakes, and the Krafla activity in recent decades included land rise, rifting and eruptions.

place: Gobabeb, Namib-Naukluft National Park, Namibia
summary: Gobabeb is a desert research station where the Kuiseb River, a large dune sea and gravel plains meet. It was founded by an Austrian entomologist and is now the Gobabeb Namib Research Institute. The page we read does not mention Mars; GSOP lists it as a reference for its large dune sea and permanent station.
terrain_geology: A dune sea lies south of the station and gravel plains lie north, with the dry Kuiseb riverbed between them.
climate: Hyperarid, with most of the little rain falling from December to May. Fog is common.
access_and_facilities: The station is southeast of the port town of Walvis Bay, inside the national park.

place: Navajo Sandstone iron concretions (Moqui marbles), Grand Staircase-Escalante region, Utah, USA
summary: Iron oxide concretions known as Moqui marbles weather out of the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone in southern Utah. A commentary in Nature noted that they look very like the hematite spherules, nicknamed blueberries, that the Opportunity rover found at Meridiani Planum. The same commentary says the Martian rocks differ in composition, and a later review says how the Utah concretions formed is still debated, which limits how far the comparison goes.
terrain_geology: The host rock is a dune-field sandstone, and the concretions are thought to have formed from groundwater that moved iron through the rock.
access_and_facilities: The monument is reached by a scenic state highway and the Hole-in-the-Rock Road from Escalante, with visitor centers in Escalante and Kanab.

place: Aquarius Reef Base, off Key Largo, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, Florida, United States
summary: Aquarius is an underwater research habitat that NASA uses for NEEMO, its long-running undersea spaceflight analog. NASA describes the focus as exploration science, spacewalk techniques and tools, and flight hardware and operations concepts. It is an analog for operations and isolation, not for terrain.
terrain_geology: The habitat sits on the seafloor next to a deep coral reef called Conch Reef.
access_and_facilities: Crews live in the habitat for the whole mission because saturation diving needs a long decompression before surfacing. Florida International University has run it since it took over from the University of North Carolina Wilmington.

place: Newberry Volcano, Newberry National Volcanic Monument, near Bend, Oregon, USA
summary: Newberry is a large volcano south of Bend, Oregon, with a caldera, a young obsidian flow and a long lava tube called Lava River Cave. NASA trained Apollo astronauts there, including future lunar landing crews. The area is now a national volcanic monument open to visitors.
terrain_geology: The summit holds a caldera that formed in a major eruption. The Big Obsidian Flow is a young glassy lava flow, and Lava River Cave is the longest continuous lava tube in the state.
climate: Precipitation falls as winter snow and summer rain, and the cave interior stays cold all year.
access_and_facilities: A paved road reaches the caldera and a gravel section leads near Paulina Peak. The Lava Lands Visitor Center runs a seasonal shuttle.

place: Ojos del Salado, Chile and Argentina border, Atacama Region (Chile) and Catamarca Province (Argentina)
summary: Ojos del Salado is the highest volcano on Earth, on the Argentina and Chile border at the southern end of the Puna de Atacama. Researchers study its gullies, crater lakes and climate as possible Mars analogues. It is a candidate in our screening and is not in our reference list.
terrain_geology: The massif is made of overlapping lava domes, lava flows, cones and many craters, mostly potassium-rich dacite. Permafrost is expected from about the middle slopes upward, with buried ice under sand and moraines.
climate: Very cold, windy and dry. Precipitation is mostly hail and snow, and the dry air keeps glaciers to small patches of firn and ice in sheltered spots.
access_and_facilities: A Chilean national route passes north of the volcano. On the Chilean side a dirt road leads to mountain refuges, and most ascents use that side.
hazards: The volcano ranks low for hazard, but summit ice means lahars are possible if it erupts.

place: Orocopia Mountains, Riverside County, California, USA
summary: The Orocopia Mountains are a desert range east of the Coachella Valley in southern California. A Caltech geology professor used the range for geologic field training of Apollo crews. We found no source stating that anorthosite occurs here, so we cannot confirm the highland rock link in the reference list.
terrain_geology: Known for Orocopia schist, a blueschist assemblage whose terrain was shaped mainly by movement on the San Andreas Fault.
access_and_facilities: The range lies south of the main interstate highway through the Colorado Desert.

place: Painted Desert and Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
summary: Petrified Forest National Park in northeastern Arizona includes part of the Painted Desert, a badland of banded, colorful clay-rich rock. The layers belong to the Late Triassic Chinle Formation. The page read does not discuss Mars; the Mars link on our list is a layered clay sequence in a dry setting that is easy to reach.
terrain_geology: The Chinle Formation contains bentonite clay that swells when wet and cracks when dry, which keeps plants from growing on the slopes.
climate: Cold semi-arid, with hot summers, freezing winters and most rain in August.
access_and_facilities: A main interstate highway crosses the park, and a park road links it to a second highway. Headquarters is east of Holbrook.
hazards: Strong winds, sandstorms and dust devils are common, and prairie rattlesnakes live in the park.

place: Pampas de La Joya, southern Peru
summary: Pampas de La Joya is a hyper-arid patch of the Atacama Desert in southern Peru. Studies of its soils report high oxidant activity using methods similar to those on the Viking and Phoenix missions, and the identity of the oxidant is still unknown. Researchers compare it with the Yungay area in Chile, noting lower organic matter at La Joya.
terrain_geology: The soils are hyper-arid desert soils, studied for their oxidants and organic content.
climate: The area is hyper-arid.

place: Payún Matrú volcanic field, Malargüe Department, Mendoza, Argentina
summary: Payún Matrú is a large volcano and volcanic field in the Andean back-arc of Mendoza province, Argentina. Its Pampas Onduladas lava flow is described as the longest Quaternary lava flow in the world. In this project it is a candidate not in our reference list, and the sources checked here do not document planetary analog use.
terrain_geology: The field's rocks range from alkali basalt to rhyolite, and basaltic volcanism has been active for a long time. Young flows are mostly rough aa lava, and the volcano has a large caldera.
climate: The climate is cold and dry with strong westerly winds.
access_and_facilities: Paved roads serve the area, with a national route to the west and another around the north and east. The volcano lies in the La Payunia provincial reserve.
hazards: The area has little water and is high and exposed.

place: Dresser Formation, North Pole Dome, Pilbara, Western Australia, Australia
summary: The Dresser Formation in the Pilbara Craton holds some of the oldest candidate traces of life on Earth, including stromatolites and other microbial structures in chert. Researchers argue that similar rocks could guide the search for life on Mars, and they cite its hot-spring deposits because Mars had silica-rich sinter at a similar time. Some researchers have challenged the biological origin of the structures.
terrain_geology: The formation forms a roughly circular ring of hills around the North Pole Monzogranite. The lowest chert unit holds barite and stromatolites, which are now mostly replaced by hematite.

place: El Pinacate and Gran Desierto de Altar Biosphere Reserve, Sonora, Mexico
summary: El Pinacate is a volcanic field of cinder cones and large craters in the Sonoran Desert, surrounded by active dunes. NASA sent Apollo astronauts here to train for walking on the Moon because the terrain resembles the lunar surface. The area is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
terrain_geology: Volcanic shield with cinder cones and a high concentration of maar craters, ringed by extensive active dunes.
access_and_facilities: The reserve lies just south of the Arizona border; Puerto Penasco, Sonoyta and San Luis Rio Colorado are the nearest cities.

place: Pisgah Crater and Lavic Lake volcanic field, Mojave Desert, California, USA
summary: Pisgah Crater is a cinder cone in the Mojave Desert and the youngest of four cones in the Lavic Lake volcanic field. Basalt flows run far from the cone across the desert floor. The page read does not describe any analog use; the Mars link on our list is a basalt flow beside a dry lake bed that can be used for calibration.
terrain_geology: Flows extend far to the west and southeast of the cone. The summit was lowered by cinder mining.
access_and_facilities: The cone sits just south of an interstate highway and the old National Old Trails Highway, west of Ludlow. The crater and much of the lava field are private property, but nearby lava tubes are a popular caving destination.

facts.label: Age of the most recent flow (argon dating)

place: Pu'u Nene cinder cone, Island of Hawaii, Hawaii, United States
summary: The cinder cone is the source of the palagonitic tephra used to make the first widely used Mars soil simulant, made at NASA's Johnson Space Center. The weathered volcanic ash contains nanophase iron oxides that give it a spectrum similar to dusty Martian deposits. The simulant has known limits: it is mostly X-ray amorphous and differs from Mars in composition.
terrain_geology: The material is weathered volcanic ash made mostly of X-ray amorphous palagonite, a hydrated alteration product of volcanic glass.
access_and_facilities: The original supply ran out and a copy was later made by Orbitec; sources say that product was no longer available some years ago (year in the facts).
hazards: The simulant is hygroscopic and is considered to have dose-dependent cytotoxicity.

facts.label: Year Orbitec simulant site taken down (reported)

place: Qaidam Basin and Dalangtan playa, Haixi Prefecture, Qinghai province, China
summary: The Qaidam Basin is a very dry basin on the north-eastern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, with salt lakes, playas and yardangs. Dalangtan is one of its four main playas, in the north-west. The China Geological Survey has studied the basin as a Mars analog, to test spectroscopy methods and equipment for China's Mars rover programme.
terrain_geology: The basin is a crescent-shaped intermontane basin ringed by the Kunlun, Qilian and Altyn-Tagh mountains, with very thick sediments. Saline lakes and playas cover about a quarter of it, and wind-carved yardangs occur in the desert.
climate: The basin is hyperarid, with cool average temperatures, very high evaporation, large daily and seasonal swings and relatively high ultraviolet radiation.
access_and_facilities: Railways cross the basin, including the Golmud to Dunhuang and Golmud to Korla lines.

place: Rio Tinto, Huelva province, Andalusia, Spain
summary: The Rio Tinto is a river in southwestern Spain with very acidic, iron-rich red water. Extremophile microbes live in it, and scientists have compared its water chemistry with the water in which the rocks at Meridiani Planum on Mars were deposited. Mining has gone on in the area for thousands of years, and it is unclear how much of the acidity is natural.
terrain_geology: The river flows through the Iberian Pyrite Belt, which has large sulphide ore deposits formed by hydrothermal activity on an ancient sea floor. Oxide terraces built by microorganisms are found well above the present water level.
access_and_facilities: Copper mining was permitted to reopen after a long pause, so parts of the area are an active mining district.
hazards: Acid mine drainage dissolves heavy metals into the water, and the article calls the river highly toxic.

place: Salar de Pajonales, Atacama Region, Chile
summary: Salar de Pajonales is a high-altitude salt flat in Llullaillaco National Park at the edge of the Atacama Desert. Low pressure, high salinity, aridity, large day and night temperature swings and strong ultraviolet light make it a model for Martian environments where life might persist. The climate here may have resembled that of Mars in its Hesperian period.
terrain_geology: A gypsum crust with domes, mounds, ridges and polygon cracks, surrounded by andesite and rhyolite rock with active hot springs.
climate: Arid and windy, with strong sunlight and low air pressure.
access_and_facilities: A road crosses the salar.
hazards: Dissolution pits and cavities in the crust can be as tall as a person.

place: Salar Grande, Tarapaca region, Chile
summary: Salar Grande is a salt flat in northern Chile that sits near the coast, unlike most Chilean salars, which are high in the Andes. Researchers treat it as an analog for Martian chloride and perchlorate deposits because very dry conditions have lasted there for a long time. Fog from the sea is the main source of water for the halite, and halite nodules there host cyanobacteria.
terrain_geology: The basin holds mostly unaltered lake-bed chloride deposits in an extensional basin, with a thick body of banded and massive halite.
climate: Hyperarid, with morning fog from the sea called camanchaca.
access_and_facilities: It lies near the city of Iquique, on the eastern margin of the Coastal Range.

facts.label: Depth of massive halite from the surface
Depth of rock salt body (at least)

place: Samail ophiolite, Wadi Tayin massif, Oman
summary: The Samail ophiolite is one of the largest and best-exposed pieces of oceanic crust and upper mantle on land. Researchers use it as an analog for Martian serpentinite environments, and one study mapped serpentine and carbonate there at fine scale as a test for orbital mineral detections. Mixed carbonate and serpentine are hard to tell apart at coarse scales, which is a caveat for the comparison.
terrain_geology: The Wadi Tayin massif has a thick mantle section of harzburgite with some dunite, overlain by gabbro, dikes and pillow lavas.
climate: The study area is semi-arid.
access_and_facilities: The Oman Drilling Project cored the crust-mantle transition and mantle peridotite in this massif.

place: Schirmacher Oasis, Queen Maud Land, East Antarctica
summary: Schirmacher Oasis is an ice-free plateau on the Princess Astrid Coast of Queen Maud Land, between the ice sheet and an ice shelf. India's Maitri Station and Russia's Novolazarevskaya Station both stand on it. In this project it is a candidate not in our reference list, and the sources checked here do not document planetary analog use.
terrain_geology: The plateau is rocky ground that supports only mosses and lichens, with more than a hundred freshwater lakes. Rock outcrops rise from the ice sheet nearby.
climate: The climate is mild for Antarctica, with a cold annual average and relatively frequent sunshine.
access_and_facilities: Maitri Station, installed in a late twentieth century programme, is a few kilometres from Novolazarevskaya and has meteorological, geomagnetic and seismological observatories. The source does not describe how the oasis is reached.

place: Hamelin Pool Marine Nature Reserve, Shark Bay, Western Australia, Australia
summary: Hamelin Pool, in World Heritage-listed Shark Bay, has the most diverse and abundant living marine stromatolites in the world. Salt levels are about double those of normal seawater, which limits animals that would graze on the microbial mats. The sources we read do not make a Mars comparison, and our list marks the site as a living-stromatolite reference that fails our water test.
terrain_geology: Shallow, salty bay water with stromatolite columns built by cyanobacteria.
access_and_facilities: The reserve is reached from the North West Coastal Highway by Hamelin Pool Road and the Telegraph Station grounds. A boardwalk is the only public access, and entry is free.
hazards: The environment is fragile, which is why public access is limited to a boardwalk.

place: Sittampundi anorthosite complex, near Salem, Tamil Nadu, India
summary: The Sittampundi complex is an outcrop of anorthosite, a rock close in composition to lunar highland rock. ISRO made its highland lunar soil simulant in bulk from rock collected here. The simulant was used at ISRO's Lunar Terrain Test Facility in Bengaluru to test the lander and rover of the Chandrayaan mission.
terrain_geology: Anorthosite rich in calcic plagioclase, with oxide proportions largely equivalent to lunar highland anorthosite according to the simulant paper.
access_and_facilities: Rock for the simulant came from the villages of Sithampoondi and Kunnamalai.

place: S P Crater and S P lava flow, San Francisco volcanic field, Arizona, USA
summary: S P Crater is a basaltic andesite cinder cone north of Flagstaff in the San Francisco volcanic field, with a long lava flow running north from the vent. Wikipedia says American astronauts have used the crater to train for moonwalking. The cone can be climbed, and the flow can be viewed from the rim.
terrain_geology: The cone has an agglomerate rim, and its lava flow comes from the same vent. Scientists debate whether the flow slightly predates the cone.
access_and_facilities: It lies north of Flagstaff, and the cone can be climbed.

place: Stillwater igneous complex, Beartooth Mountains, southern Montana, United States
summary: The Stillwater complex is a large layered mafic intrusion. Its anorthosite and norite are the raw material for NASA's NU-LHT lunar highland regolith simulants, which are based on the average composition of Apollo highland soil samples. A newer simulant made by Washington Mills uses the same Stillwater rock approach.
terrain_geology: The complex is a layered mafic intrusion exposed along the north flank of the Beartooth Range. It has chromium ore and has been mined for palladium and other platinum group elements.
access_and_facilities: The simulant feedstock comes from the Stillwater Mine near Nye, Montana.

place: Sudbury Basin, Greater Sudbury, Ontario, Canada
summary: The Sudbury Basin is the eroded remnant of a very old impact crater in Ontario. NASA used it to train Apollo astronauts to recognise impact-formed rocks such as breccias. Trainees included the crews of three Apollo landing missions.
terrain_geology: Main rock units include footwall breccia, the Sublayer, the Sudbury Igneous Complex and the Whitewater Group. The basin's ores hold nickel, copper, gold, silver and platinum-group metals, mostly on the outer rim.
access_and_facilities: The city of Greater Sudbury sits on the basin's southern edge.

place: Tenoumer crater, western Sahara, Mauritania
summary: Tenoumer is a small impact crater in the Sahara Desert of Mauritania, formed in Precambrian gneiss and granite. A volcanic origin was once proposed, but current evidence indicates an impact origin. It is a candidate in our screening and is not in our reference list, and the source we read does not describe it as an analog site.
terrain_geology: Basalt and rhyodacite occur outside the crater basin. Sediments cover the crater bottom, and the rim stands well above the floor.

place: Tirez lagoon, central Spain
summary: Tirez was a small, seasonal, very salty lagoon in central Spain that dried out completely. Researchers monitored its drying for about a quarter of a century and propose it as a time-resolved analog for the wet to dry transition on early Mars. The sources we read do not confirm the sulfate chemistry listed in the reference list.
terrain_geology: A shallow closed-basin lagoon with very high salt content. A neighbouring lagoon in the same system is described as rich in salt and sulphur.
climate: Alternating dry and wet periods over about two decades before total drying.

place: Tottori Sand Dunes, Tottori Prefecture, Japan
summary: The Tottori Sand Dunes are a long coastal dune system on the Sea of Japan. A lunar demonstration field opened on the grounds of Tottori University's Arid Land Research Center, where companies and researchers can test lunar rovers and other equipment. A published study found the dune sand has mechanical properties closer to lunar regolith than the sand in many test facilities.
terrain_geology: Sediment from the Chugoku Mountains was carried by the Sendai River to the sea and shaped by wind into dunes, with bowl-shaped hollows and wind ripples.
access_and_facilities: The dunes lie just outside Tottori city. The demonstration field has flat, slope and free-design zones.

place: Umm as Samim sabkha, eastern edge of the Rub al Khali, Oman
summary: Umm as Samim is a very large salt flat at the foot of the Oman Mountains where groundwater collects. Its crust looks solid but can give way, and locals call it the Mother of Poisons. We found no Mars analog literature specific to this site; Mars analog work in the region has focused on the Samail ophiolite and the Abu Dhabi sabkha.
terrain_geology: The flat is a salt marsh with a brackish crust and little vegetation, fed by drainage from the mountains and the wadis.
climate: The setting is a desert with little vegetation.
access_and_facilities: Wilfred Thesiger travelled through the area on his Oman journey.
hazards: The crust can break and trap vehicles and people, like quicksand.

place: Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, Katmai National Park and Preserve, Alaska, USA
summary: The Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes is an ash-filled valley in Katmai National Park, formed by the Novarupta eruption in the early twentieth century, the largest eruption by volume of that century. NASA and the USGS trained Apollo astronauts there in two groups. Vegetation still does not grow on the valley floor.
terrain_geology: The valley is filled with ignimbrite and ash deposits. Early steam vents gave the valley its name, though few remain active.
access_and_facilities: Visitors usually take a bus along the only road in the park, which starts at Brooks Camp.
hazards: The area has five active stratovolcanoes nearby, which the Alaska Volcano Observatory monitors.

place: White Sands National Park, Tularosa Basin, New Mexico, USA
summary: White Sands protects part of the largest gypsum dunefield on Earth. Gypsum dunes on Mars are known from Olympia Undae near the north pole, and researchers have used White Sands to study how gypsum sand moves and sorts. A recent conference abstract proposes White Sands measurements as ground truth for the Martian dunes.
terrain_geology: Gypsum from ancient seas was dissolved by rain and carried into the basin, where wind breaks the crystals into sand. Lake Lucero is a dry lakebed in the southwest, and the Alkali Flat is a remnant of an ice age lake.
climate: Cold semi-arid climate, with hot summer afternoons and cold winter nights.
access_and_facilities: The park lies on the north side of a main highway, southwest of Alamogordo, and is surrounded by White Sands Missile Range.
hazards: The park and the highway close during missile tests, and errant missiles have fallen inside the park.

place: Wolfe Creek crater, Great Sandy Desert, Western Australia, Australia
summary: Wolfe Creek is a large, well-preserved meteorite crater in the Great Sandy Desert of northern Western Australia. It is known as Kandimalal to the Djaru people. Wikipedia calls it arguably the second most obvious meteorite crater on Earth after Barringer Crater; the page does not describe it as a lunar analog.
terrain_geology: An exposed, undrilled impact structure with iron meteorite fragments and iron oxide shale balls around it.
access_and_facilities: The crater lies in a national park south of Halls Creek and is reached by the Tanami Road.

place: Norris Geyser Basin, Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming, USA
summary: Norris Geyser Basin is described in an NPS-derived listing as the hottest, oldest and most dynamic thermal area in Yellowstone. Unlike most basins in the park, its water is acidic. Mars researchers compare silica deposits near Home Plate in Gusev crater with hydrothermal settings on Earth, but the sources read do not tie Norris to Mars in particular, and one study argued that El Tatio in Chile is a closer match than Yellowstone.
terrain_geology: The basin lies near the northwest edge of the Yellowstone caldera and builds silica sinter around vents. It includes Steamboat Geyser, the tallest active geyser in the world.
access_and_facilities: Boardwalks and marked trails serve the basin from the park's main loop road.
hazards: Several people have died after falling into hot springs, so visitors must stay on boardwalks and marked trails.
